title: Type 1 Diabetes in Adults: Newly Diagnosed Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with new-onset hyperglycaemia and suspected or confirmed type 1 diabetes in the emergency department, ward or diabetes clinic: recognising and treating diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at presentation, confirming the diagnosis, starting basal-bolus insulin, hypoglycaemia treatment, self-monitoring, education, inpatient insulin, and the first-year screening and follow-up plan, using Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) protocols with NICE NG17 as a labelled supplement.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The MOH DKA/HHS protocol (Protocol 005) is written for adults over 14 years in wards outside intensive care; it does not apply to patients who are haemodynamically unstable or weigh 50 kg or less, and those patients need critical-care input. The protocol text and its order sheet differ slightly: the text lowers the insulin rate to 0.05 units/kg/hour when glucose is below 6 mmol/L, while the order sheet switches to dextrose 5% in saline when glucose is below 13 mmol/L; both are shown as printed.

The MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines (Protocol 018) are written for clinical pharmacists in ambulatory diabetes clinics and quote American Diabetes Association-style recommendations; their insulin dose estimates (0.3 to 0.5 units/kg a day), 500 and 1,700 rules and hypoglycaemia table are used as stated. The document carries no publication date in the extracted text.

The MOH documents do not give an autoantibody or C-peptide pathway for confirming type 1 diabetes, do not set a type 1 HbA1c target separate from the general adult target (below 7%, or 6.5% to 8% for selected patients), do not describe continuous glucose monitoring or insulin pumps beyond naming continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion, and do not give retinopathy, foot or thyroid screening intervals. Those points come from NICE NG17 and are labelled.

NICE NG17 (UK) sets an HbA1c target of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower with fasting glucose 5 to 7 mmol/L and pre-meal 4 to 7 mmol/L; the MOH guideline uses HbA1c below 7% and pre-prandial 80 to 130 mg/dL (4.4 to 7.2 mmol/L). The two are shown side by side; local SHC or MOH diabetes policy decides.

NICE NG17 advises against aspirin for primary prevention in type 1 diabetes, while the MOH pharmacy guideline says it may be considered in increased cardiovascular risk after discussion; the conflict is shown and not resolved here.

NICE NG17 prefers twice-daily insulin detemir as basal insulin and notes that Levemir (detemir) is being discontinued in the UK (supply end expected December 2026); availability in Saudi Arabia and the MOH formulary should be checked before choosing detemir.
Insulin degludec, insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitoring are mentioned in NICE NG17 but no MOH dose or criteria were found; only the principle is stated.

Dose figures in the MOH pharmacy guideline carry no stated renal or hepatic adjustments except those in the inpatient basal-bolus protocol (0.25 units/kg a day total in chronic kidney disease not on dialysis); other adjustments are not given and the product monograph applies.

Sick-day rules are only named in the MOH documents; the specific steps (never stop basal insulin, check glucose and ketones every 3 to 4 hours, fluids) are from the inpatient basal-bolus note that type 1 diabetes needs basal insulin at all times, NICE ketone-monitoring advice, and general teaching, and need local confirmation.

The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine and insulin brand was not verified; check hospital formulary.

Source texts were read through automated extraction (MOH PDFs converted to text; the NICE page converted from HTML) rather than page by page in the originals, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune loss of insulin-producing beta cells; without insulin the body breaks down fat to ketones and DKA follows; people with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes often present with DKA (MOH DKA/HHS protocol). Saudi Arabia has one of the highest incidences of type 1 diabetes in the world (over 35,000 people, about 3,900 new cases a year, highest in the Riyadh region), and DKA is very common at first presentation (MOH DKA/HHS protocol). DKA is the biochemical triad of ketonaemia, hyperglycaemia and acidaemia; treatment is rehydration, insulin, potassium and electrolyte balance, and treatment of the trigger (MOH DKA/HHS protocol). Insulin needs fall sharply once glucose toxicity clears and a honeymoon phase follows, so early doses must be adjusted from glucose readings (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines). Most people need multiple daily injections of basal and mealtime rapid-acting insulin; mixed insulin is only for those who cannot manage this (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines; NICE NG17).

symptoms: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, weakness (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, which track with acidosis severity (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Drowsiness or confusion in severe DKA.
Hunger, sweating, shakiness or confusion after starting insulin (hypoglycaemia) (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
physicalSigns: Dehydration: dry mucosa, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Kussmaul breathing and acetone breath in DKA (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Reduced consciousness in severe DKA or HHS (Glasgow Coma Scale below 12 is a severity marker).
Weight loss, often a low or normal body mass index and young age, though age or body mass index alone must not exclude type 1 diabetes (NICE NG17 1.1.1 to 1.1.2).
redFlags: Glucose 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more, ketones positive (blood, or 2+ or more urine) and venous bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or pH below 7.3: DKA; start fluids and insulin protocol now (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

Severe DKA markers: Glasgow Coma Scale below 12, pH below 7.1, ketones above 6 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L, potassium below 3.3 or above 6.0 mmol/L, systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg, oxygen saturation below 92% with pulse above 100 or below 60, urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour or acute kidney injury: manage in high-dependency or intensive care (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Serum potassium below 3.3 mmol/L: give potassium first and hold insulin until potassium is 3.3 mmol/L or more (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Haemodynamic instability or body weight 50 kg or less: do not use the ward protocol; involve intensive care (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Plasma glucose above 30 mmol/L with osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and no ketoacidosis suggests hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, not DKA: separate protocol (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Hypoglycaemia with altered consciousness (level 3): glucagon 1 mg intramuscular or intravenous glucose (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines; NICE NG17 1.9.11).
Missed basal insulin in hospital: a patient with type 1 diabetes must have basal insulin at all times to avoid ketosis (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
precipitants: Infection (the commonest precipitant) and missed insulin doses (MOH DKA/HHS protocol; MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
Marked stress, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, stroke, corticosteroids (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
New diagnosis of diabetes (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Irregular eating, extra exercise, alcohol or too much insulin (hypoglycaemia triggers) (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

differentials.condition: Type 2 diabetes presenting with hyperglycaemia or ketosis
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Older, overweight, slower onset; but type 2 diabetes can present with DKA after prolonged hyperglycaemia or a stressor; do not exclude type 1 diabetes by age or body mass index alone, and treat ketosis with insulin (MOH DKA/HHS protocol; NICE NG17 1.1.2).

Glucose above 30 mmol/L, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, pH above 7.3, bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L, no or trace ketones, mostly older adults with type 2 diabetes and more severe dehydration (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Autoantibodies negative and presentation not typical; revisit the diagnosis at later reviews (NICE NG17 1.1.3).

differentials.condition: Starvation or alcoholic ketosis, sepsis, acute abdomen
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ketones without marked hyperglycaemia or another cause of acidosis; DKA itself can mimic an acute abdomen and alters white cell count, temperature and the electrocardiogram (MOH DKA/HHS protocol; NICE NG17 1.10.4).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more with symptoms; fasting 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms diabetes; with ketones decides DKA (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines; MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: First minutes: new hyperglycaemia, exclude DKA
actions: Check capillary glucose and blood or urine ketones in every adult with new hyperglycaemia or suspected type 1 diabetes (NICE NG17 1.10.2).

Take a venous gas for pH and bicarbonate, urea and electrolytes, creatinine, full blood count, urinalysis and culture, chest X-ray, electrocardiogram and troponin if indicated; send blood cultures if infection suspected (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Confirm DKA when all three are present: glucose 200 mg/dL or more (or known diabetes), positive ketones, and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or pH below 7.3 (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

Check for severity markers (GCS below 12, pH below 7.1, ketones above 6 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L, potassium below 3.3 or above 6.0, systolic below 90 mmHg, oxygen saturation below 92%, urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour) and send severe cases to high-dependency or intensive care (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
If the patient is unstable or weighs 50 kg or less, do not use the ward protocol; call intensive care (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
If no ketosis and the patient is well, move to starting subcutaneous insulin (below); do not delay insulin in a patient with ketones because glucose is only moderately raised.

clinicalManagement.title: DKA treatment: fluids, insulin, potassium
actions: Fluids: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour with no potassium, 1 L over the next 2 hours, then 1 L over the next 4 hours with potassium as below; the text gives 15 to 20 mL/kg/hour or 1 to 1.5 L in the first hour; then 100 to 250 mL/hour; be careful in elderly, young and cardiac patients; replacing fluid too fast risks cerebral oedema (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

Insulin: do not start until the potassium result is available and potassium is 3.3 mmol/L or more; mix 50 units human regular insulin in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride and infuse at a fixed rate of 0.1 units/kg/hour with no bolus; check glucose hourly; continue the usual long-acting insulin if the patient takes one (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

When glucose falls below 6 mmol/L reduce the infusion to 0.05 units/kg/hour; when below 13 mmol/L change the fluid to dextrose 5% in saline at 100 to 250 mL/hour; if below 4 mmol/L give 25 mL dextrose 50% bolus (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

Potassium (passing urine and normal renal function): above 5.2 mmol/L none; 3.3 to 5.2 mmol/L add 40 mmol per litre of fluid and do not exceed 10 mEq an hour; below 3.3 mmol/L hold insulin, apply a cardiac monitor, do an electrocardiogram, and give 40 mEq potassium chloride in 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride over 4 hours (maximum 10 mEq/hour); resume insulin when potassium is 3.3 mmol/L or more (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

Bicarbonate is not routine; give only if pH is below 6.9 and not responding: 50 mmol in 200 mL over one hour (200 mL/hour), repeat every 2 hours until pH is above 6.9, hold if potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, and check potassium every 2 hours (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Find and treat the precipitant, record input and output and daily weight, and give venous thromboembolism prophylaxis if consciousness is reduced (MOH DKA/HHS protocol; NICE NG17 1.10.11).

Switch to subcutaneous insulin when bicarbonate is 18 mmol/L or more and/or pH 7.3 or more, the anion gap is closed and the patient can eat; overlap the first rapid-acting dose with the infusion for one hour (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Start basal-bolus insulin
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as ketosis resolves or at once if not in DKA
actions: Use multiple daily injections of basal and mealtime rapid-acting insulin analogue for newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes; do not use twice-daily mixed insulin as first choice (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines; NICE NG17 1.7.1 to 1.7.2).

Total daily dose: 0.3 to 0.5 units/kg actual body weight at the start; 0.2 to 0.5 units/kg in the honeymoon phase; 1.0 to 1.5 units/kg with ketosis, during illness or growth; adjust from glucose readings because requirements fall rapidly once glucose toxicity clears (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Split about half as basal insulin (a conservative approach reduces the calculated basal dose by 20%) and half as rapid-acting insulin divided between three meals, each premeal dose then adjusted individually (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Carbohydrate ratio by the 500 rule (500 divided by total daily dose gives grams of carbohydrate per unit of rapid-acting insulin; 450 rule for regular insulin); correction factor by the 1,700 rule (1,500 for regular insulin) (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Rapid-acting analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) are given about 15 minutes before or with the meal; regular insulin 30 minutes before; do not routinely inject rapid-acting analogue after meals (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines; NICE NG17 1.7.11).

Teach injection technique, rotation of sites and storage: unopened insulin in the refrigerator at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius, in-use vial or pen at room temperature for 3 to 6 weeks (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, as printed).

clinicalManagement.title: Insulin while in hospital (non-critical)
actions: Patients with type 1 diabetes must have basal insulin ordered at all times, even if nil by mouth, to avoid ketosis (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).

Total daily insulin by weight: 0.25 units/kg in chronic kidney disease not on dialysis; 0.3 units/kg if underweight (BMI below 18.5), age 65 or over or on haemodialysis; 0.4 units/kg normal weight; 0.5 units/kg overweight; 0.6 units/kg or more if obese, on glucocorticoids or insulin-resistant; half basal, half bolus divided at meals; reduce basal by 25% if nil by mouth, poor intake or well controlled (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).

Hold bolus insulin if nil by mouth or eating less than about 80% of calories; give correction doses from the low, medium or high scale; target glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL; adjust basal every 1 to 3 days by fasting glucose (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
Total parenteral nutrition: add 1 unit of regular insulin per 10 g dextrose (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Hypoglycaemia plan
actions: Teach the symptoms (sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion, blurred vision, anxiety); some people have none at night (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Conscious patient: 10 to 20 g rapidly absorbed carbohydrate (for example 3 to 4 glucose tablets, half a cup of juice or regular soda, 1 tablespoon of sugar), repeat in 15 to 20 minutes if glucose is still below 70 mg/dL or symptoms persist, then a meal or snack (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Unconscious patient: glucagon 1 mg subcutaneously or intramuscularly (response in about 6.5 minutes), or admit; check response at 10 minutes and give intravenous glucose if not improving, then oral carbohydrate when safe (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines; NICE NG17 1.9.11).

Look for the cause: irregular meals, extra exercise, alcohol, too much insulin, gastroparesis; consider reducing insulin by 10 to 25% after unexplained hypoglycaemia (MOH DKA/HHS protocol; MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

clinicalManagement.title: Education and self-management
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before discharge and in the first weeks
actions: Educate on insulin type, dose, time and storage, lifestyle, glycaemic targets, adherence, self-monitoring and dose adjustment, acute complications (hypoglycaemia, DKA) and sick days; refer to a diabetes educator for injection technique (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, Follow Up Pathway for Type 1 diabetes).

Self-monitor at least 4 times a day (before each meal and bed); more often when ill, before and after sport or if hypoglycaemia is frequent; offer carbohydrate-counting training and consider continuous glucose monitoring (NICE NG17 1.6.19 to 1.6.20, 1.6.10, 1.3.1 to 1.3.5).

Sick-day rules: never stop basal insulin, check glucose every 3 to 4 hours, check ketones when ill or glucose is high, drink fluids, and seek urgent care for vomiting, ketones or drowsiness (MOH inpatient note on basal insulin; NICE NG17 1.10.1; see gaps).
Driving and occupational advice, and psychological wellbeing: ask about both at diagnosis (NICE NG17 1.1.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Baseline assessment and screening
actions: Examine feet and eyes, weight and body mass index, blood pressure; measure urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, eGFR, lipid profile and TSH (NICE NG17 1.1.11, 1.14.39).
Refer immediately to the local eye screening service at diagnosis (NICE NG17 1.14.5).

From 5 years after diagnosis check urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR yearly, twice yearly if albumin above 30 mg/g or eGFR below 60; use an ACE inhibitor or ARB for hypertension with albuminuria (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
Assess for coeliac disease if unexplained weight loss and be alert to other autoimmune disease (Addison's disease, pernicious anaemia) (NICE NG17 1.11.1 to 1.11.2).

Treat blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg (below 130/80 mmHg with albumin-to-creatinine ratio 70 mg/mmol or more), start a renin-angiotensin blocker first for hypertension, and review statin use and smoking (NICE NG17 1.12; MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

regimens.indication: Basal insulin in basal-bolus regimen for newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes
regimens.dose: About 50% of the total daily dose (total daily dose 0.3 to 0.5 units/kg at the start); a conservative start is 20% below the calculated 50%
regimens.frequency: Once daily at the same time each day (bedtime or morning)
regimens.duration: Long term; adjust every 1 to 3 days by fasting glucose
adjustments: Less nocturnal hypoglycaemia than NPH; more injection-site pain (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Chronic kidney disease not on dialysis: total daily insulin 0.25 units/kg; age 65 or over, underweight or on haemodialysis: 0.3 units/kg; reduce basal by 25% if nil by mouth or well controlled (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
Converting from glargine U-100 to U-300: start with the same dose, a higher dose may be needed (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
Pregnancy: US pregnancy category C (MOH Table 2).
Hepatic impairment: not stated in the MOH documents; check the product monograph.
monitoring: Fasting capillary glucose daily; HbA1c every 3 to 6 months (NICE NG17 1.6.1); hypoglycaemia review (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
contraindications: Do not omit basal insulin in type 1 diabetes even when nil by mouth or ill (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.

Dose reduction as for glargine in chronic kidney disease, older adults, underweight or nil by mouth (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).

regimens.indication: Mealtime and correction insulin in basal-bolus regimen
regimens.dose: About 50% of the total daily dose divided equally into three meals at the start, then adjusted; carbohydrate ratio by the 500 rule; correction by the 1,700 rule
regimens.frequency: Before or with each meal (15 minutes before for lispro and aspart; with the meal in the inpatient protocol); correction doses before meals and at bedtime
adjustments: Hold if nil by mouth, on total parenteral nutrition or eating less than about 80% of requirements (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).

Correction scale by size: sensitive (BMI below 25 or total daily dose below 50 units), average (BMI 25 to 30 or 50 to 90 units), resistant (BMI above 30 or above 90 units); start low-dose in renal dysfunction, hypoglycaemia unawareness, insulin-naive patients and older adults (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
Pregnancy: lispro and aspart US category B; glulisine category C (MOH Table 2).
Do not routinely inject after meals (NICE NG17 1.7.11).
monitoring: Pre-meal and bedtime capillary glucose; adjust each dose from the next reading (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.

regimens.patientGroup: Adults over 14 years with DKA, haemodynamically stable
regimens.dose: 50 units human regular insulin in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride; 0.1 units/kg/hour with no bolus; 0.05 units/kg/hour when glucose is below 6 mmol/L
regimens.duration: Until bicarbonate 18 mmol/L or more and/or pH 7.3 or more, anion gap closed, patient able to eat; overlap the first rapid-acting dose for one hour
adjustments: Do not start until potassium is known and 3.3 mmol/L or more; hold if potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L until replaced (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
If glucose falls below 4 mmol/L give 25 mL dextrose 50% or add dextrose 10%; below 13 mmol/L change fluid to dextrose 5% in saline (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Do not use in unstable patients or patients 50 kg or less.
Continue usual long-acting insulin (glargine or detemir) at the same time if the patient uses it (MOH order sheet, optional).
Renal, hepatic and pregnancy adjustments are not stated in the protocol.
monitoring: Capillary glucose hourly (2-hourly if 5 to 10 mmol/L for 3 consecutive hours); venous gas and electrolytes at the intervals set on the order sheet; potassium every 2 hours with bicarbonate (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.
regimens.sourceTitle: Saudi Ministry of Health: DKA/HHS Protocol (Adult), Protocol 005
regimens.sourceEdition: MOH DKA/HHS protocol, Section Insulin and Order Sheet

regimens.indication: Fluid resuscitation in adult DKA (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg or more)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults over 14 years with DKA, over 50 kg
regimens.dose: 1 L over the first hour (no potassium), 1 L over the next 2 hours, 1 L over the next 4 hours with potassium; then 100 to 250 mL/hour; 15 to 20 mL/kg/hour in the first hour as printed in the text; 0.45% sodium chloride 4 to 14 mL/kg/hour if hypernatraemic
regimens.duration: Until euvolaemic; replace half the estimated water deficit over 12 to 24 hours
adjustments: Caution in elderly, very young and cardiac patients (risk of fluid overload); over-rapid replacement risks cerebral oedema (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Change to dextrose 5% in saline at 100 to 250 mL/hour when glucose is below 13 mmol/L (MOH order sheet).
Haemodynamic instability: do not use the ward protocol.
monitoring: Vital signs and Glasgow Coma Scale, input and output, daily weight, serum electrolytes (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.
regimens.sourceTitle: Saudi Ministry of Health: DKA/HHS Protocol (Adult), Protocol 005
regimens.sourceEdition: MOH DKA/HHS protocol, Section Fluid therapy and Order Sheet

regimens.patientGroup: Adults over 14 years with DKA, passing urine, normal renal function
regimens.dose: Serum potassium above 5.2 mmol/L: none; 3.3 to 5.2 mmol/L: 40 mmol per litre of fluid, maximum rate 10 mEq an hour; below 3.3 mmol/L: hold insulin and give 40 mEq in 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride over 4 hours (maximum 10 mEq/hour)
regimens.duration: Until potassium is in the normal range and the infusion is no longer needed
adjustments: Only if the patient is passing urine and has normal renal function (MOH order sheet).
Change the concentration whenever potassium is rechecked; apply a cardiac monitor and do an electrocardiogram for potassium below 3.3 mmol/L.
Request a higher-concentration infusion from pharmacy if needed (MOH order sheet).
monitoring: Potassium every 2 hours while on bicarbonate and at the intervals on the order sheet; electrocardiogram if below 3.3 mmol/L (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.
regimens.sourceTitle: Saudi Ministry of Health: DKA/HHS Protocol (Adult), Protocol 005
regimens.sourceEdition: MOH DKA/HHS protocol, Section Potassium Therapy and Order Sheet

regimens.indication: Severe acidosis not responding to initial DKA treatment (pH below 6.9)
regimens.dose: 50 mmol in 200 mL water at 200 mL/hour
regimens.frequency: Repeat every 2 hours until pH is above 6.9
adjustments: Not routinely needed; hold if potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
NICE NG17 1.10.6 (labelled): do not generally use bicarbonate in DKA.
monitoring: Potassium every 2 hours while infusing; venous pH (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.
regimens.sourceTitle: Saudi Ministry of Health: DKA/HHS Protocol (Adult), Protocol 005

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with type 1 diabetes unable to take oral treatment
regimens.frequency: Single dose; repeat only per local policy
regimens.duration: Single dose, then oral carbohydrate when able to swallow
adjustments: Generally given intramuscularly in the outpatient setting; mean response time about 6.5 minutes (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
Check response at 10 minutes and give intravenous glucose if consciousness is not improving; observe for relapse (NICE NG17 1.9.11, labelled).
Pregnancy, renal and hepatic adjustments are not stated; check the product monograph.
monitoring: Capillary glucose before each meal and at bedtime, and any time symptoms occur; severe hypoglycaemia needs review of the regimen (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, Section Complications; NICE NG17 1.9.14).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.
regimens.sourceTitle: Saudi Ministry of Health: Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, General Administration of Pharmaceutical Care (Protocol 018)
regimens.sourceEdition: MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, Section Complications, Table 6

regimens.indication: Level 1 and 2 hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient
regimens.genericName: Oral rapid-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets, juice, sugar)
regimens.dose: 10 to 20 g of rapidly absorbed carbohydrate (examples of 15 g: 3 to 4 glucose tablets, half a cup of juice or regular soda, 1 tablespoon of sugar)
regimens.frequency: Repeat in 15 to 20 minutes if glucose remains below 70 mg/dL or symptoms persist
regimens.duration: Until glucose is above 70 mg/dL, then a meal or snack
adjustments: No renal, hepatic or pregnancy adjustment is stated.
monitoring: Capillary glucose before each meal and at bedtime, and any time symptoms occur; severe hypoglycaemia needs review of the regimen (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, Section Complications; NICE NG17 1.9.14).
contraindications: The MOH documents do not list contraindications for this medicine beyond what is shown; check the product monograph.

regimens.sourceEdition: MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines, Section Complications, Table 5

medicationPlan.note: Insulin starting doses, the 500 and 1,700 rules, hypoglycaemia treatment, DKA infusion rates, potassium replacement and inpatient doses are from the MOH documents. NICE NG17 is used for basal insulin choice, monitoring and screening and is labelled. Brand availability and SFDA registration were not verified. The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine and insulin brand was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more; 2-hour 75 g glucose tolerance test 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more; random glucose 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms; HbA1c 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more; confirm by repeat if clear hyperglycaemia is absent (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

Glucose 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more or known diabetes; positive serum ketones or urine ketones 2+ or more; venous or arterial bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or pH below 7.3 (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).
Venous bicarbonate 18 mmol/L or more and/or pH 7.3 or more, closed anion gap, and able to eat; overlap the first rapid-acting dose for one hour with the infusion (MOH DKA/HHS protocol).

Level 1: below 70 and 54 mg/dL or above (3.9 and 3.0 mmol/L); level 2: below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L); level 3: severe event with altered mental or physical status needing assistance (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).

HbA1c below 7% (6.5% for selected low-risk patients; 8% if history of severe hypoglycaemia, limited life expectancy or advanced complications); pre-prandial capillary glucose 80 to 130 mg/dL (4.4 to 7.2 mmol/L); peak postprandial below 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) (MOH Diabetes Pharmacotherapy Clinic Guidelines).
HbA1c 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower, individualised; 5 to 7 mmol/L on waking; 4 to 7 mmol/L before meals; 5 to 9 mmol/L 90 minutes after meals (NICE NG17 1.6.22 to 1.6.23).
Capillary glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL (7.8 to 10.0 mmol/L) (MOH inpatient basal-bolus protocol).

teaching.scope: Adult with new-onset hyperglycaemia and suspected or confirmed type 1 diabetes in the emergency department, ward or diabetes clinic: recognising and treating diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at presentation, confirming the diagnosis, starting basal-bolus insulin, hypoglycaemia treatment, self-monitoring, education, inpatient insulin, and the first-year screening and follow-up plan, using Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) protocols with NICE NG17 as a labelled supplement.
learningObjectives: Recognise and treat DKA at presentation and confirm type 1 diabetes.
Calculate a starting basal-bolus insulin dose and teach self-management.
Plan hypoglycaemia treatment, inpatient insulin and the first-year screening.
pitfalls: Starting insulin before potassium is known.
Omitting basal insulin because the patient is nil by mouth.
Using bicarbonate routinely or giving fluids too fast.
Excluding type 1 diabetes because of age or body mass index alone.
Using mixed insulin as first choice in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes.
keyPoints: DKA needs glucose 200 mg/dL or more, ketones and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or pH below 7.3; hold insulin until potassium is 3.3 mmol/L or more.
Starting insulin is 0.3 to 0.5 units/kg a day, half basal and half mealtime; type 1 diabetes always needs basal insulin.
Treat hypoglycaemia with 10 to 20 g of carbohydrate, glucagon 1 mg if unconscious.

patientEducation: Type 1 diabetes needs insulin every day for life; you must never stop basal insulin, even if you are ill or not eating.
Check your glucose before meals and at bedtime, and check ketones when ill or when glucose is high.
Carry fast-acting sugar; your family should know how to give glucagon.
Go to the emergency department for vomiting, abdominal pain, fast breathing, drowsiness or positive ketones.
Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use insulin can be kept at room temperature for the time on the label.
lifestyleAndDiet: Balanced meals with carbohydrate counting, regular physical activity with glucose checks before and after, no smoking, limit alcohol (it can cause late hypoglycaemia).
Regular eye, foot, kidney and dental review; vaccinations as per national schedule.
mdtReferrals: Endocrinologist or diabetologist; diabetes educator and nurse; clinical pharmacist (diabetes pharmacotherapy clinic); dietitian; ophthalmology (eye screening); podiatry; psychologist; emergency or intensive care team for DKA; obstetrician for pregnancy.
dischargeCriteria: Discharge after DKA has resolved (bicarbonate 18 mmol/L or more or pH 7.3 or more, closed anion gap), the patient is on subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and eating, can inject and monitor, has a hypoglycaemia plan, glucagon and sick-day rules, the precipitant is treated, and review in the diabetes clinic is booked within days.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Diabetes team review within days of discharge for insulin titration; HbA1c every 3 to 6 months; annual review of eyes, feet, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR (yearly after 5 years' duration in MOH guidance), blood pressure, lipids, TSH, injection sites and hypoglycaemia awareness; sooner after any DKA or severe hypoglycaemia.
